entry.title: A better Figure 3
entry.content:
How to read it

Each hidden state is drawn in two dimensions. The horizontal position is the shared direction, which decides whether the old answers or the new answers win. The vertical position is the fact’s own part, which picks its answer within that region. A fact is answered when it sits on its own spot.

The three phases

Before finetuning, the old facts sit on their spots and the new facts are unknown.

In the collapse, the new facts all answer in the same region, so their errors agree and add up to one push that moves every hidden state the same way. The old facts are carried into the wrong region together. Some new facts already reach their spots.

In the recovery, each new fact learns its own part. With normalization the length of every hidden state is fixed, so a long shared shift leaves less room for the own parts. Once the new facts depend on their own parts, the shift is pulled back and most old facts return to their region. Without normalization nothing pulls the shift back, and the old facts stay out.

In the erosion, single old facts drift off their own spots. This slow loss is specific to each fact and is the part of the forgetting that does not come back.

The old facts were never erased. During the collapse they moved as one group and kept their own parts, which is why the recovery needs no replay of old data.
entry.summary: A schematic of the three phases of finetuning, with and without normalization, showing where the old and the new facts land and which ones are answered.

entry.title: Why did OLMo recover old facts in only one experiment?

link.title: Why did OLMo recover old facts in only one experiment?

entry.content:
I think the strongest result comes from the experiment with the small Transformer. After training on new facts, the model starts to favor the same set of answers across many old questions. When the authors remove this shared bias from the answer scores, the model answers most of those questions correctly again. It does this without training on the old facts a second time.

My main concern is why OLMo recovered some old facts in one experiment but not in the other. The authors train two copies of OLMo on different data. One learns facts about fictional people, such as where they work. The other learns who makes real products. Both start making mistakes on old facts. With more training, the first model gets some of those facts right again. The second does not show the same recovery.

The authors suggest that the difference comes from a clue in the new data. A fictional person’s name gives no clue about an employer chosen at random. But if the model recognizes a product as a car, it can narrow down the list of manufacturers. Favoring car companies helps it answer questions about several products, so it has a reason to keep that bias.

I find this explanation plausible, but the experiment changes two things at once: how useful the clue is and how much the model already knows about the subject. For example, the model might recognize a car and know where it is sold without knowing who makes it. Learning its manufacturer adds one fact about a familiar product. A fictional person, on the other hand, is someone the model has never seen before. From these two runs alone, we cannot tell whether recovery depends on the clue, on how familiar the subject is, or on both.

I would test this using the same fictional products and the same four manufacturers in both runs. In the first run, two companies make cameras and the other two make speakers. Knowing the product type narrows the answer down to two companies. In the second run, I would shuffle the assignments so that each company makes cameras and speakers equally often. I would keep the wording, the amount of training, and the number of examples per company the same. If accuracy on old facts recovers more in the second run, that would be stronger evidence that the clue itself affects recovery.

This matters in practice: when a model starts making mistakes on facts it used to know, the paper does not yet show how to tell whether more training will bring those answers back.
entry.summary: A critique of what the two OLMo training runs tell us about recovery and how to test the explanation.

entry.title: Papers worth knowing this week
entry.content:
This week’s paper argues that much of what looks like forgetting during finetuning is a reversible loss of access rather than lost knowledge. The five papers below approach the same question from different directions: the paper that named the phenomenon, one on why some finetuning methods forget less, one on when models stop being able to absorb new facts without overwriting old ones, one separating forgetting in the features from forgetting in the output layer, and one on how pretraining length affects finetuning.

The paper that named it

Spurious Forgetting in Continual Learning of Language Models (Zheng et al., ICLR 2025). Shows that performance drops in continual learning often reflect a loss of task alignment in the first optimization steps rather than a loss of knowledge, and proposes freezing the bottom layers as a remedy. This week’s paper builds directly on it, and suggests that its shared shift toward the new answers may be one concrete form of that loss of alignment.

Why some finetuning forgets less

RL’s Razor: Why Online Reinforcement Learning Forgets Less (Shenfeld et al., 2025). At equal performance on the new task, reinforcement learning preserves prior capabilities better than supervised finetuning, and the amount of forgetting is predicted by the KL divergence between the finetuned and base model on the new task; on-policy RL is implicitly biased toward the KL-minimal solution. It gives a distribution-level account of forgetting, where this week’s paper gives a geometric one.

When replay is enough, and when it is not

Forgetting in Language Models: Capacity, Optimization, and Self-Generated Replay (Marek et al., 2026). Samples a language model generates from its own training distribution work as replay data and nearly eliminate forgetting, unless the model was pretrained close to saturation and has no capacity left; without replay, low learning rates reduce forgetting at the cost of many more steps. It complements this week’s finding that higher learning rates deepen the collapse.

Features stay, heads collapse

Heads Collapse, Features Stay: Why Replay Needs Big Buffers (Lanzillotta et al., ICLR 2026). Separates deep forgetting, in the features, from shallow forgetting, in the classifier: a tiny replay buffer keeps the features linearly separable, but fixing the classifier needs a much larger one. It is the image-classification counterpart of this week’s result that the old facts keep their relative geometry while only the readout loses them.

Pretraining length and adaptability

Overtrained Language Models Are Harder to Fine-Tune (Springer et al., ICML 2025). Longer pretraining can make a model worse after finetuning: the instruction-tuned OLMo-1B pretrained on 3T tokens scores over 2% lower on several benchmarks than its 2.3T-token counterpart, because its parameters become more sensitive to any modification. It raises a question this week’s paper leaves open: whether the shared, recoverable part of forgetting changes with pretraining budget.
entry.summary: Five recent papers on forgetting during finetuning, each answering a different part of the question this week's paper raises: when is lost knowledge really gone?

entry.title: Papers worth knowing this week
entry.content:
A DEAFENING SILENCE: CATASTROPHIC FORGETTING LIVES IN THE OUTPUT EMBEDDINGS OF TOKENS THE DATA NEVER SPEAKS: These guys make some claims about why and where forgetting occurs. The main one is that optimizing a single paramater (Adam’s epsilon) may reduce 50%+ in catastrophic forgetting.

Do LLMs Really Forget? Hidden-State Leakage in Model Unlearning and How to Fix it Claim is that “forgetten” information is often hidden in intermediate layers. They purpose an interesting mechanism, probe intermediate layers, train train the probe to reconstruct forgotten answers, update the llm to make the probes fail(min-max).
entry.summary: A single-line optimizer adjustment may serve as the primary defense against catastrophic forgetting.

The original

The figure is difficult to follow because you have to start in the middle, follow either the left or right branch, return to the middle, and then follow the other branch.

The redesign

This figure is much easier to follow because it follows the conventional left-to-right reading direction. Once you finish reading the first row from left to right, you can naturally move on to the second row.

What changed and why

Rearranging the items in the figure to follow the conventional left-to-right reading direction makes the figure much easier to read and understand.

entry.title: Rewriting Section 2 - Forgetting that undoes itself

link.title: Rewriting Section 2 - Forgetting that undoes itself

entry.content:
What I changed and why

Mainly the ordering: setting first, then each finetuning set with its outcome, then the evidence and leading questions. This flow seemed more natural, given section 2 is between the introduction and the results.

Before and after

Before 2 FORGETTING THAT UNDOES ITSELF To understand when forgetting is not catastrophic, we first need a setting in which it clearly is not: one in which performance collapses, yet the knowledge demonstrably survives (Appendix C.1). We use synthetic biographies (Allen-Zhu & Li, 2024), on which spurious forgetting was identified (Zheng et al., 2025), as they let us control what the model knows before finetuning and what it learns during it. A transformer is pretrained on two non-overlapping sets of biographies, A and B, in a single stage rather than one per set (Zheng et al., 2025), until it recalls all of their facts, and is then finetuned on biographies of new individuals, without any replay. We compare two sets of new biographies, C and B′ , which differ only in how they overlap with the old ones. We describe how they are built, and what overlapping means precisely, in Section 4; for now, the only relevant property is that C overlaps with both A and B, while B′ overlaps only with B (Figure 1, middle). Finetuning on C yields classical catastrophic forgetting behavior (Figure 1, left): as the new facts are learned, recall of both A and B declines slowly and steadily. Finetuning on B′ barely affects recall of B, but recall of A follows a strikingly different trajectory (Figure 1, right), in three phases that we refer to throughout the paper: – Collapse: recall of A quickly drops, well before the new facts are learned. – Recovery: recall of A then partially returns as the new facts are acquired, although A never reappears in training. – Erosion: finally, recall of A declines slowly and persistently, as in catastrophic forgetting. This trajectory raises two questions: why finetuning on B′ hides the facts of A while sparing those of B, and why the collapse reverses on its own. Section 3 answers both in a minimal model. Section 4 then returns to Transformers, and to the biography structure needed for the phenomenon to appear.
After 2 FORGETTING THAT UNDOES ITSELF We study forgetting in two settings: a minimal associative memory model (Cabannes et al., 2024), which allows the mechanism to be analyzed (Section 3), and a controlled Transformer (Section 4), a more realistic setting. We use synthetic biographies (Allen-Zhu & Li, 2024), on which spurious forgetting was identified (Zheng et al., 2025), as they let us control what the model knows before finetuning and what it learns during it. We pretrain on two non-overlapping sets of biographical facts, A and B, where for each attribute (e.g., birthplace, employer, etc.), A's answers are drawn from half of the possible vocabulary and B's from the other half. We then finetune on a third set of biographies of new individuals, without any replay of the individuals of A and B. We compare two sets of new finetuning biographies, C and B′, which differ by how their vocabulary overlaps with the disjoint vocabularies of A and B (Figure 1, middle). When the answers of the new individuals are drawn only from B's half, we call the set B′. Finetuning on B′ barely affects recall of B, but recall of A follows a strikingly different trajectory (Figure 1, right), in three phases that we refer to throughout the paper: - Collapse: recall of A quickly drops, well before the new facts are learned. - Recovery: recall of A then partially returns as the new facts are acquired, although A never reappears in training. - Erosion: finally, recall of A declines slowly and persistently, as in catastrophic forgetting. When the answers are drawn from both parts of the vocabulary, we call the set C. Finetuning on C yields classical catastrophic forgetting behavior (Figure 1, left): as the new facts are learned, recall of both A and B declines slowly and steadily. **The knowledge is hidden, not erased** At the bottom of the collapse in the B′ finetuning scenario, only 12% of A's facts are recalled, yet 86% still rank their correct answer first among the answers in their own half (Appendix C.1). Finetuning on B′ thus gives a setting in which forgetting clearly is not catastrophic: one in which performance collapses, yet the knowledge demonstrably survives. This trajectory raises two questions: why finetuning on B′ hides the facts of A while sparing those of B, and why the collapse reverses on its own. Section 3 answers both in a minimal model. Section 4 then returns to Transformers, and to the biography structure needed for the phenomenon to appear.

The general rule

Help readers orient by introducing the variables before showing results, so the next sections follow naturally. Keep each condition next to its outcome.
entry.summary: One sentence that makes people want to click.

entry.title: Applying AIDA for Communication
entry.content:
What’s AIDA?

Slide posts are basically the modern day slideshow. They can help present complex scientific topics, using an easy-to-digest and engaging format.

The AIDA method is used by many to maximize engagement and impact. In short, the structure is:

  • Attention. Why should the viewer care? A strong hook to attract readers.
  • Interest. The majority of the post. Should normally be the context. Try to maintain the interest of the reader.
  • Desire. The main value of the post.
  • Action. An action for the viewer. Read more in our blog, engage in the comment sections, etc.

Writing AIDA slides

You may use the slides template I’ve created or change it to your liking, but try keeping a standard format. Canva Link

Platforms usually include: X (4-6 slides in a thread), LinkedIn (4-10 slides as a PDF), and Instagram (4-10 slides).

Discussion: Should we open an Instagram account? As slides are commonly used on Instagram, LinkedIn and X might already have more of our target academic audience. Although such accounts do exist on Instagram, such as @ourworldindata and @quantamag.

Examples for posts

Here are some ideas for posts:

  • Everything you need to know about [insert paper idea]. Slides Explaining the paper. May contain a visualization made by someone.
  • Points we had to discuss about [insert paper name]. 3-5 slides about the main points discussed in class. Each slide contains a different point.
  • This is how you can improve your graphs (based on the graphs from [insert paper name]). Slides showcasing someone’s graph, what improved and how the reader can use this knowledge.
  • How [insert writing rule] can help your writing. Slides about an actionable writing rule, ending with showcasing someone’s writing.

I’ll link my own posts later on this week.

Sources that helped me

  • ‘From traditional science posters to social media slides with the AIDA framework’. A blog post about using AIDA as scientists.
  • ‘Why Your Instagram Carousels Are Being Ignored— Use AIDA technique’. A video about the AIDA method.
entry.summary: What's AIDA and how can we use it to improve course communication. Including a Canva template.

entry.title: 3 Follow-Ups: Understanding and Preventing Spurious Forgetting

link.title: 3 Follow-Ups: Understanding and Preventing Spurious Forgetting

entry.content:
Follow-ups worth doing

The paper demonstrates that forgetting during fine-tuning does not necessarily imply a loss of knowledge. Instead, a common shift in internal representations can temporarily interfere with retrieving previously learned facts (Spurious Forgetting). This raises several questions about what determines forgetting, whether it extends beyond factual knowledge (like mathmatical or coding abilities), and how we might prevent it.

1. Does generalization come at the cost of remembering?

Research question: How does the semantic structure of newly learned knowledge affect spontaneous recovery?

In Section 5.1, the authors of the paper observe spontaneous recovery when the new facts are arbitrary associations, but not when they are semantically meaningful. They suggest that a possible explanation for that is that shared information remains useful for predicting meaningful associations, potentially reducing the incentive to reverse the common shift (caused by fine-tuning).

However, the two datasets differ in more than just their semantic structure.

Proposed experiment: Construct a controlled dataset of subject-answer pairs and gradually increase the proportion of randomly shuffled answers. For example, assign fictional individuals hometowns that are consistent with their countries of origin, and progressively shuffle these assignments. This would allow us to vary the predictability of the answers while keeping the subjects, answer vocabulary, dataset size, and answer frequencies fixed.

Measure the magnitude of the common shift and the extent of spontaneous recovery at different levels of semantic structure, comparing models at similar new-fact accuracy.

Why it is worth doing: This experiment could help establish whether semantic structure itself determines the persistence of forgetting (we could see if there is a trend to the level of forgetting as semantic structure changes, rather than just comparing 2 extreme cases like the paper examined). It would also investigate a potentially counterintuitive trade-off between learning generalizable patterns and preserving access to previously learned knowledge.

2. Do language models forget abilities or just facts?

Research question: Does the mechanism of spurious forgetting extend beyond factual recall to more complex tasks and abilities?

The paper focuses on factual associations, but as we know, language models also acquire abilities such as mathematical reasoning, programming, and logical inference. It remains unclear whether the deterioration of these abilities during fine-tuning can arise from the same geometric mechanism.

Proposed experiment: Evaluate a pretrained language model on factual recall but also on mathematical reasoning, and programming tasks. Fine-tune it on an unrelated domain, such as history, and measure the deterioration of each capability. Then apply the SVD-based intervention introduced in Section 5.2 of the paper and evaluate the extent to which each capability recovers, without retraining on the original tasks.

Compare the model’s performance before and after the SVD modification, and investigate whether removing other singular components (not only the dominant one) can also restore previously learned abilities.

Why it is worth doing: Recovering complex abilities through targeted low-rank weight interventions would provide evidence that the mechanism extends beyond associative memory. This could have practical implications for developing specialized language models without sacrificing previously acquired capabilities.

3. Can we prevent forgetting by changing the order of training?

Research question: What if we deliberately organize the training data so that the gradients are less aligned? Can controlling gradient alignment during fine-tuning reduce the common representational shift responsible for spurious forgetting?

The mechanism described in Section 3 of the paper suggests that shared structure across training examples produces aligned updates, which collectively shift old representations and interfere with the retrieval of knowledge. This raises the possibility of controlling the shift by organizing the training examples.

Proposed experiment: Fine-tune identical models on the same dataset using three mini-batch constructions:

  • Random batching: standard random sampling.
  • Homogeneous batching: grouping semantically similar examples together.
  • Diverse batching: deliberately combining examples from different semantic groups.

The hypothesis is that diverse batches could reduce the alignment of interfering gradient components, thereby limiting the common shift.

Measure gradient similarity, the magnitude of the common shift, and accuracy on both old and new facts throughout training. Compare the strategies at matched new-fact accuracy to ensure that less forgetting is not simply a consequence of less learning.

Why it is worth doing: While the authors use SVD to recover old knowledge after forgetting has occurred, this approach aims to reduce forgetting in the first place. If it would be successful, then changing how training examples are grouped into mini-batches could help preserve old knowledge without modifying the model architecture, adding parameters, or retraining on old data.
entry.summary: Exploring how semantic structure, learned abilities, and training dynamics influence spurious forgetting.

entry.title: Multi-Stream Attention Residuals in a thread

link.title: Multi-Stream Attention Residuals in a thread

entry.content:
X / Twitter

The residual stream in a Transformer is secretly attention over DEPTH. Every past layer gets dumped into one vector with a frozen weight of 1. Make it multi-head and you get a 1.58× compute speedup for +0.5% extra FLOPs. New paper: Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR). 🧵

2/ Why deep stacks waste depth: h₍l+1₎ = h₍l₎ + f(h₍l₎). Later layers read the accumulated sum, not individual earlier features. A feature born in layer 3 is hard to retrieve at layer 40. And as the stream grows, each new update shrinks relative to it. Depth dilutes itself.

3/ That additive sum IS attention along the layer axis. Just single-head, with fixed uniform weights. Hyper-Connections = a recurrent linear-attn depth memory. AttnRes = single-head softmax retrieval over depth. The obvious next step: multi-HEAD depth attention.

4/ The trap: split the hidden state into head fragments like normal MHA and it breaks. In depth attention the retrieved “value” is the hidden state itself. Slice it and you destroy its integrity. The paper tried it and performance dropped.

5/ MSAR’s move: pull head diversity from the SEQUENCE axis instead. Expand each layer output into m full-dim streams via cheap causal depthwise 1-D convs (kernels 4/8/12). Each head attends over depth through a different contextual view. Diverse heads, every one full-dimensional.

6/ Results (DeepSeekMoE-style, 18B & 28B MoE): MSAR wins all 12 benchmarks at both scales. 28B avg 52.4 vs AttnRes 49.4 vs vanilla 44.6. Iso-loss speedup: 1.58× vs 1.35× (AttnRes), 1.30× (mHC). Overhead: +0.5% FLOPs, +0.3% params.

7/ The ablation that proves the mechanism: delete the convolutions (keep the extra query heads) and the gain mostly vanishes, 1.847 → 1.862 loss. The win comes from source diversity, not from more query heads. A hand-built AttnRes+mHC hybrid can’t match it either.

8/ Mental model: a deep network is doing retrieval over its own history. Spending compute on better depth-wise retrieval beats simply adding parameters. A free 1.58× quality-per-FLOP. Paper: arXiv 2610.13630 (SJTU × Xiaohongshu Dots Studio).

Bluesky

The residual connection is a disguised attention mechanism over the depth axis: single-head, with frozen uniform weights. MSAR generalizes it to multi-head. The catch: you can’t channel-split the heads, because the “value” in depth attention is the whole hidden state, so slicing breaks it. 🧵

2/ Fix: get head diversity from the sequence axis. Expand each layer output into m full-dimensional streams with cheap causal depthwise 1-D convs (kernels 4/8/12). Each head attends over depth through a different contextual view. +0.5% FLOPs, and it stores only single-stream summaries, expanded on demand.

3/ On 18B/28B MoE it wins all 12 benchmarks and hits a 1.58× iso-loss compute speedup (vs 1.35× AttnRes, 1.30× mHC). Ablation: remove the convs and the gain collapses. It’s source diversity, not extra queries. arXiv 2610.13630.

Mastodon

New architecture paper worth knowing: Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR).

The pitch: the residual stream h₍l+1₎ = h₍l₎ + f(h₍l₎) is secretly attention over the depth axis, single-head with fixed uniform weights. Later layers read an accumulating blob and dilute their own depth. MSAR makes depth attention multi-head.

You can’t channel-split the heads, because the value in depth attention is the full hidden state. So MSAR draws diversity from the sequence axis: cheap causal depthwise 1-D convs expand each layer output into m full-dim views.

Result: +0.5% FLOPs, wins all 12 benchmarks at 18B/28B MoE, 1.58× iso-loss compute speedup. arXiv 2610.13630.

#NLProc #MachineLearning

LinkedIn

A 1.58× compute speedup hiding in the residual connection

One of the most overlooked parts of a Transformer is also one of the oldest: the residual connection, h₍l+1₎ = h₍l₎ + f(h₍l₎). Most of us treat it as plumbing. A new paper, Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR) from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Xiaohongshu’s Dots Studio, argues it’s doing something much richer, and that we’ve been doing it in the crudest possible way.

The insight: that additive sum is a form of attention along the depth axis, where every earlier layer’s output is retrieved with a fixed, uniform weight of 1. That’s why very deep models use depth inefficiently. Later layers read one accumulated vector rather than individual earlier features, and each new layer’s contribution shrinks relative to the growing stream.

Prior work (Hyper-Connections, Attention Residuals) had already started treating depth as something to attend over. MSAR takes the natural next step, multi-head depth attention, and solves the problem that blocked it. You can’t split the hidden state into head fragments the way sequence-axis attention does, because in depth attention the “value” is the hidden state itself. MSAR instead builds diverse heads from the sequence axis, using lightweight causal convolutions to give each head a different contextual view of the same layer output.

Why a practitioner should care: at 18B and 28B Mixture-of-Experts scale, MSAR wins all 12 evaluated benchmarks and delivers a 1.58× iso-loss compute speedup over a standard residual baseline, for +0.5% training FLOPs. The lineage it builds on (mHC, AttnRes) is already used in trillion-parameter training runs, so this is a live production architecture, not a research toy.

The broader lesson: where you spend compute can beat how much you add. Better depth-wise retrieval is nearly free quality per FLOP, which is exactly the kind of lever that matters when you’re compute-bound.

Paper: arXiv 2610.13630.

Notes

Images per post

  • Hook (1/) and LinkedIn header: the headline bar chart, MSAR vs Vanilla/mHC/AttnRes 12-benchmark average at 18B/28B.
  • 3/: the “residual stream = attention over layers” schematic (HC = linear-attn memory, AttnRes = single-head, MSAR = multi-head).
  • 5/: the multi-stream source-expansion figure (one layer output, m conv views, per-stream depth attention, Hpre fusion).
  • 6/ and 7/: the iso-loss scaling curve and the ablation table.

Who to tag Authors: Qin, Zhang, Dai, Zou, Wu, Yang, Xia, Yao, Liu, Yan (Shanghai Jiao Tong University / Xiaohongshu “Dots Studio”). Pull their handles from the arXiv page (2610.13630) before tagging. Worth looping in the Hyper-Connections and Attention Residuals authors too, since this builds directly on their line.

Success metrics

  • Hook: impressions, profile visits, and clicks on the arXiv link.
  • Thread retention: how many readers reach post 6/ (the results).
  • Reposts and quote-posts from people working on architecture; author engagement counts more than raw impressions.
  • LinkedIn: comments from engineers, not just likes.

entry.title: Papers worth knowing this week
entry.content:
Theme this week: most of “training” is one shift. Two of these show RL and self-improvement collapsing onto a single activation or weight edit, which lines up directly with our spurious-forgetting read (the reversible “common shift”) and the JEPA audit’s representation-vs-reward split. The third is the attention-architecture line we were on with MSAR.

  1. RL Post-Training in Diffusion Transformers Is Activation Steering — A single fixed steering vector recovers 90 to 96% of the reward gain from policy-gradient RL post-training using 65× fewer parameters than LoRA, so most of what RL “learns” here is one constant activation shift. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26627

  2. Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights — A 27B model acts as its own optimizer, diagnosing its wrong answers and editing its own weights through forward passes only (no backprop), keeping the edits that survive a few practice problems. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21885

  3. On-Policy Morphing into Hybrid Attention Models — FlashMorph2 converts a pretrained Transformer into a full/linear-attention hybrid by scoring candidate layer configurations end to end on the model’s own hidden states while co-adapting the weights, beating proxy-based conversion. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24809

Pick if we only read one: the activation-steering paper. It is the sharpest version of the pattern we keep hitting (one shift explains the gain), and it is a short, concrete read.
entry.summary: A run of trending papers keeps finding the same thing — a lot of what we call "training" turns out to be one shift in activations or weights, plus a clean attention-architecture conversion that lands next to our MSAR read.
